basic_identification.sector_category: Petroleum, Coal and Related Products (approved by the Petroleum, Coal and Related Products Division Council; finalized by the Plastic Containers Sectional Committee) [1]

scope.summary: This standard prescribes the requirements, methods of sampling, and test methods for infant plastic feeding bottles and receptacles [2]. It covers bottles and accessories (excluding teats) manufactured from virgin polypropylene, polyethersulfone (PES), olefin-based polymers, or co-polyesters [3, 4]. The standard explicitly bans and excludes the use of polycarbonate (PC) due to safety concerns regarding Bisphenol A (BPA) leaching [5, 6], and prohibits polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) [3, 7]. Rubber teats are excluded from direct material specification here and must separately conform to IS 3565 [3, 7].

amendment_slips.description: Deletes drinking accessory and single-use definitions (Clauses 3.2, 3.12); modifies Clause 4 to mandate virgin polypropylene (IS 10910), PES, or other approved safe olefin-based polymers; prohibits PVC, PET, and Bisphenol A (BPA); directs food-grade requirements for silicone teats; removes Figure 1 (drinking accessories); adjusts drop test repetitions to 10 free falls on both base and side; and updates sample prep exclusions for ageing resistance [4, 7, 9, 10].

Inserts IS 3025 (Part 2) : 2004 for element determination using ICP-AES spectroscopy; updates chemical extraction parameters to exclude the bottle's hood from testing; and replaces Table 1 with an updated schedule of maximum heavy metal limits and test methods [11-13].

certification_and_marking.certification_status: Strict Statutory Mandatory Certification. Under Section 11(2) of 'The Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottle and Infant Foods (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1992' (as amended in 2003), it is a criminal offence to sell or otherwise distribute any feeding bottle in India unless it carries the BIS Standard Mark (ISI Mark) affixed directly to its container [27].

requirements.detail: The bottles must carry the Standard Mark of the Bureau of Indian Standards (ISI Mark) on their packaging container to legally permit sale and distribution in the Indian market [27, 28].

The materials used must be entirely Bisphenol A (BPA) free. The standard completely deletes polycarbonate (PC) as an eligible raw material for infant feeding bottles due to dangerous toxic leaching risks [3, 5-7].

The product packaging must display the following exact warnings for childcare safety: 'Always use this product with adult supervision', 'Always check food temperature before feeding', and 'Keep all components not in use out of the reach of children' [29, 30].

Each carton must be permanently marked with the source of manufacture, nominal capacity, batch and code number, month and year of manufacture, plastic material type (food-contact grade), and recycling product symbol conforming to IS 14534 [26, 31].

To carry the combined ISI and ECO-Mark, the manufacturer must produce official pollution control clearances under the Water Act of 1974, Air Act of 1981, and Environment Protection Act of 1986. The packaging must be biodegradable or recyclable, and a list of ingredients must be displayed in descending order [10, 32-34].

plain_language_summary.summary: IS 14625:2015 is the strict national Indian safety standard for the manufacture, quality evaluation, and statutory marking of infant plastic feeding bottles and receptacles. Because infant health is highly vulnerable, Indian law (specifically the IMS Act of 1992) prohibits the sale or distribution of any baby feeding bottle unless it is certified with the BIS Standard Mark. In this revision, polycarbonate materials have been entirely banned due to hazardous Bisphenol A (BPA) leaching risks, limiting acceptable plastic materials to safe food-grade alternatives such as virgin polypropylene or polyethersulfone. When auditing these products, engineers must double-check mechanical and physical integrity parameters, including the 1.2 m free-fall drop test (repeated 10 times on the base and 10 times on the side), maximum overall chemical migration limit compliance, minimum 70% light transmittance, and ensure the mandatory warning statements regarding adult supervision are prominently printed.
